international.pageDescription: What you need to start working here — the paperwork, the authorities and the language.
international.checkedNote: This information was checked against the authorities’ own websites on {{date}}. The rules change — always check with the authority before making a decision.

validation.title: Does what you already know count here?
validation.description: If you have education or a profession from another country, there are two things to sort out: what your education corresponds to here, and whether your profession requires a Swedish licence.

uhr.title: Have your education assessed
uhr.body: The Swedish Council for Higher Education (UHR) assesses education from other countries and writes a statement of what it corresponds to in Sweden. It is free of charge, and you can attach the statement when you apply for jobs or studies. UHR assesses upper secondary education, post-secondary vocational education and higher education.
uhr.tip: Do not have your certificates any more? Apply anyway — UHR explains on their site what can be done when documents are missing.

regulated.title: Does your profession require a licence?
regulated.body: Some professions you may not work in without a Swedish licence, however much experience you have. This includes many jobs in healthcare and teaching. In that case the professional authority assesses your education — not UHR.
regulated.health: Healthcare: the National Board of Health and Welfare decides on licences and protected professional titles. The route differs depending on whether you were educated inside or outside the EU/EEA, and the Swedish language requirement is high — the level is stated on their site.
regulated.teacher: Schools and preschools: the Swedish National Agency for Education decides on teacher certification.
regulated.other: Not sure whether your profession is regulated — start with UHR and ask the Public Employment Service. They know who assesses what.
regulated.healthLink: National Board of Health and Welfare — licensing

permit.title: Do you need a work permit?
permit.eu: If you are a citizen of an EU/EEA country or of a Nordic country you do not need a work permit. You may start working straight away, and you should not contact the Migration Agency — move on to the next tab.
permit.thirdCountry: If you are a citizen of a country outside the EU/EEA a work permit is usually required, and as a rule you apply before travelling here. If you already live here with a residence permit on other grounds, different rules may apply.
permit.noNumbers: We deliberately do not state any amounts or processing times here. They change every year, and an outdated figure on this page could cost you a permit. The Migration Agency always has what applies right now.
permit.linkException: Migration Agency — who may work without a permit

next.body: Once you know what your education corresponds to: write it in your CV with the Swedish equivalent in brackets, so a Swedish employer understands what they are reading.

firstNote.title: Read this first
firstNote.body: Almost everything else requires you to be registered as a resident and to have a personal identity number. That takes time — count on several weeks. Until then you cannot get a BankID, and many services require BankID. It is not you doing something wrong; that is how the system fits together.

folkbokforing.title: Report that you have moved to Sweden
folkbokforing.body: You do not apply for a personal identity number — you report your move to the Tax Agency and are registered as a resident. The number comes with that registration. It requires that you plan to live here for at least a year. You report the move in the Tax Agency’s e-service, at the earliest 14 days before you move, and you must then visit a service office in person to prove who you are. Book a time in advance.

samordningsnummer.title: Staying for less than a year?
samordningsnummer.body: Then you will not get a personal identity number, but you may instead get a coordination number. It is applied for separately, and some services work less well with it. The Tax Agency explains the difference.

idkort.title: Get an ID card
idkort.body: The Tax Agency’s ID card requires that you are registered as a resident. The fee must be paid before you book a time, and you bring the receipt to the appointment. You also need to prove your identity — either with an approved ID document or with a person who vouches for who you are.

bankkonto.title: Open a bank account
bankkonto.body: You have the right to a payment account with basic functions if you are legally resident within the EEA. Not having a personal identity number is not in itself a reason for the bank to say no. If you are refused anyway you are entitled to it in writing — and you can then turn to the bank’s complaints officer and on to the National Board for Consumer Disputes.

bankid.title: Get a BankID
bankid.body: You order BankID from your bank, so it requires that you have an account. A great deal in Sweden requires BankID. If you do not have one, Freja is an alternative at some authorities — ask when you are there.

forsakringskassan.title: Tell the Social Insurance Agency you have moved
forsakringskassan.body: You do not register in general — you report that you have moved here. It matters above all if you move with children, want a European Health Insurance Card, or are going to apply for a benefit. Whether you are insured follows from living or working here.

vardcentral.title: Choose a health centre
vardcentral.body: You choose which health centre you want to belong to. That is who you call when you fall ill, and they refer you onwards if needed.

sfi.title: Sign up for Swedish for immigrants (sfi)
sfi.body: Sfi is free of charge for you who are 16 or older, live in the municipality and do not already know basic Swedish. You sign up with your municipality. Once you are registered as a resident, the municipality must be able to offer you a place within three months.
sfi.linkLabel: National Agency for Education — about sfi

validering.title: Have your education assessed
validering.body: UHR writes a free statement of what your education corresponds to in Sweden. It is often what makes an employer understand what you can do.

arbetsformedlingen.title: Register with the Public Employment Service
arbetsformedlingen.body: Register as early as you can. It affects what support and what benefits you can get, and some programmes require that you have been registered for a while.

akassa.title: Join an unemployment insurance fund
akassa.body: Membership is voluntary and you pay a monthly fee. The benefit depends on how long you have been a member and how much you have worked — which is why it pays to join early, even if you do not need it now.

korkort.title: Is your driving licence valid here?
korkort.body: A driving licence from the EU/EEA is valid in Sweden. If your licence is from another country, different rules apply and there are time limits. The Transport Agency has what applies for your country.

skatt.title: Check your tax table
skatt.body: When you get a job, tax is deducted according to a table that depends on where you live. If the deduction is wrong you can apply for an adjustment with the Tax Agency, so you do not pay too much or too little during the year.

pension.title: Your pension after moving here
pension.body: If you have worked in another country you may have earned a pension there. The Swedish Pensions Agency can tell you what applies between Sweden and that country.

language.title: Swedish
language.description: You do not have to wait until your Swedish is solid to apply for jobs. But it opens doors, and here are the routes.
language.levelsTitle: How good does your Swedish need to be?
language.levelsBody: It depends on the job. In many jobs the employer decides, and everyday Swedish goes a long way. In a few professions the requirement is regulated — for a healthcare licence the National Board of Health and Welfare requires a high level of Swedish.
language.sfiBody: Sfi is divided into four courses (A, B, C and D) and three study paths, where the path is chosen according to your previous schooling. That structure is not the same as the European scale A1–C2, and there is no official translation between them. Ask your municipality which course suits you.

tips.t1: Say what you can, even if it comes out wrong. You learn faster by speaking than by waiting until it is right.
tips.t2: Listen to the news in easy Swedish for a while every day — the same words keep coming back.
tips.t3: Set your phone to Swedish. You read it a hundred times a day anyway.
tips.t4: Practise the ten phrases above out loud before you go to an interview.
tips.t5: Ask someone to correct you. Most people are happy to if you ask.

linkedin-profile.question: Is your LinkedIn profile up to date?
linkedin-profile.tip: A filled-in profile is found by recruiters more often than a half-finished one. Headline, about text and experience go a long way.

linkedin-photo.question: Do you have a profile photo?
linkedin-photo.tip: LinkedIn themselves say profiles with a photo get more views. An ordinary, clear picture of your face is enough — it does not need a photographer.

linkedin-headline.question: Does your LinkedIn headline say what you do or are looking for?
linkedin-headline.tip: The headline is the first thing anyone sees. "Care assistant looking for something new" says more than "Open to opportunities".

google-search.question: Have you ever searched for your own name?
google-search.tip: Many people look up whoever they are about to meet. Worth knowing what comes up — usually nothing, and that is an answer too.

personal-website.question: Do you have somewhere to show what you have done?
personal-website.tip: It does not have to be a website. A collection of work samples you can link to in an application is enough.

share-content.question: Do you share anything about your field on LinkedIn?
share-content.tip: Sharing something you have read now and then means more people see your name. There is no set rhythm — do it when you have something to share.

own-content.question: Have you written anything of your own — a post or a text?
own-content.tip: A short post about something you know is enough. You do not have to be an expert to have something to say.

engage-others.question: Do you comment on or like other people’s posts?
engage-others.tip: Replying to others is often easier than writing your own — and it shows up for their network.

expertise-shown.question: Does what you know come through in what you write?
expertise-shown.tip: Concrete experience from jobs you have had says more than general advice.

active-network.question: Do you keep in touch with people in your field?
active-network.tip: Many jobs are filled because someone knows someone — how many cannot be said with certainty, but contacts are rarely wasted.

industry-events.question: Do you go to industry meet-ups or other gatherings?
industry-events.tip: Meeting in person usually makes more of an impression than a message. One occasion now and then is enough.

mentors.question: Do you have someone to ask for advice about working life?
mentors.tip: It does not have to be a formal mentor. A former colleague or manager you can get in touch with counts.

recommendations.question: Do you have recommendations on LinkedIn?
recommendations.tip: Recommendations from others carry more weight than what you write about yourself. Most people say yes if you ask.

consistent-message.question: Do your CV and your LinkedIn say roughly the same thing?
consistent-message.tip: The same job words in both places makes what you say recognisable — and makes you easier to search for.

unique-value.question: Can you say briefly what you are good at?
unique-value.tip: Two sentences is enough. It is the kind of thing you work out by writing it down, not by thinking about it.

target-audience.question: Do you know what kind of employer you want to reach?
target-audience.tip: Knowing who you are writing for makes both texts and applications easier to put together.

createCV.q: How do I create a CV?
createCV.a: Go to the CV section and follow the step-by-step guide. You can choose from different templates and get AI help with the wording.

interestGuide.a: The Interest Guide helps you find careers that match your personality and interests. It takes about 10 minutes to complete.

saveJobs.a: When searching for jobs, you can click the heart/save button on each job ad to save it to your job tracker.

multipleCVs.q: Can I have multiple CV versions?
multipleCVs.a: Yes! You can save multiple versions of your CV and choose which one to use for each application.

aiWriter.q: How does the AI letter writer work?
aiWriter.a: The AI analyzes the job ad and your CV to write a cover letter that matches that specific job.

atsAnalysis.a: ATS (Applicant Tracking System) is software that many companies use to filter CVs. Our analysis helps you optimize your CV to get past these systems.

howToSearch.q: How do I search for jobs through the portal?
howToSearch.a: Use the job search function to search among job openings. You can filter by location, profession, and employment type.

saveVsApply.q: What's the difference between saving and applying?
saveVsApply.a: When you save a job, it's added to your job tracker so you can return to it later. Applications are usually made through the company's website.

jobAlerts.q: Can I get notifications about new jobs?
jobAlerts.a: Yes, you can set up job alerts in your settings to receive emails when new jobs matching your criteria are published.

knowledgeBase.q: What can I do in the Knowledge Base?
knowledgeBase.a: The Knowledge Base contains articles, guides, and tips about everything from CV writing to interview techniques and labor law.

exercises.a: The exercises are interactive tools that help you practice various aspects of job searching, like selling yourself or preparing for interviews.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.description: What you might wonder about before getting started.
faq.a1: Jobin is always free for participants. Organizations pay a fixed license of 2,990 SEK/month plus 290 SEK per active consultant. No hidden fees – all features included.
faq.q2: I've been job searching for a long time without results. Can Jobin really help me?
faq.a2: Absolutely. Many of our users have been long-term unemployed and have, with the help of our structured tools and personal guidance, gotten back to work. You're not alone, and there are paths forward. The tools are specially designed to provide support even when things feel tough.
faq.q3: I don't even know what I want to work with. Where should I start?
faq.a3: Start with our interest guide! It helps you explore your strengths and interests, and gives suggestions for careers that might suit you. No pressure – just discovery. Many users have discovered new career paths they never thought of before.
faq.a4: Yes, we take your privacy very seriously. Your information is stored securely with modern encryption on servers in the EU and is never shared with third parties without your consent. If you choose to use AI features, your texts are sent to our AI provider OpenRouter for processing, which takes place in the USA — you explicitly consent to this the first time, and you can use the portal without AI. You always own your data and can delete your account at any time. We follow GDPR and have clear procedures for data security.
faq.q5: How does the AI help in the CV generator work?
faq.a5: Our AI analyzes your experience and suggests improvements in text, structure, and keywords. It helps you formulate your strengths in a way that both recruiters and automated systems (ATS) appreciate. You always have full control and can edit everything.
faq.q6: Can I use Jobin on my phone?
faq.a6: Yes! Jobin is fully responsive and works great on mobile, tablet, and desktop. You can search for jobs, update your CV, and do interview training wherever you are.

relevance.title: Is LinkedIn the right channel for you?
relevance.body: LinkedIn is strongest in office work, IT, finance, engineering and public administration. If you are looking for work in care, warehousing, retail, construction, cleaning or restaurants, jobs are usually filled another way — through the employer’s own site, staffing agencies, the Swedish Public Employment Service, or by getting in touch directly. A profile can still help people find you, but spend most of your time where the jobs are actually filled.

negotiation.description: How to prepare for the salary conversation — step by step, with room to write down what you decide.
negotiation.swedishMarketDesc: In many sectors a collective agreement sets the framework for pay, and salaries are usually reviewed once a year in a salary conversation. If you belong to a union they can give you data and support.

preparation.title: Preparation
preparation.description: Most of it is settled before the meeting starts.
tips: Find out roughly what others get for similar work
Write down what you can do and have done — including internships, studies and volunteering
Decide on a level you aim for and a lowest level you would accept
Ask your union whether they have salary statistics for the occupation
phrases: “I have looked at what similar roles pay, and I land around …”
“What I bring into the role is …”

opening.title: Opening
tips: Say early that you want to talk about pay, so neither of you has to wonder
Let the other side name a figure first if you can
Keep your notes in front of you — that is perfectly fine
Breathe. Silence after a question is not yours to fill
phrases: “I am looking forward to starting. Shall we cover pay as well?”
“What did you have in mind for this role?”

case.title: Your case
case.description: Explain why the level is reasonable.
tips: Start from the work and what you contribute, not from your private finances
Give examples rather than judgements about yourself
Mention what is hard to replace: languages, a driving licence, certificates, experience of that setting
If you have been away from work — say what you did during that time
phrases: “In my last job I did … and it led to …”
“Given what the role requires, I am thinking …”

apart.title: If you land apart
apart.description: A counter-offer is not a no.
tips: Ask for time to think — you do not have to answer the same day
Ask what it would take to get higher, and when you can revisit it
Things other than money can be negotiated: hours, training, wellness, travel, permanent contract
If you are far apart, ask how they arrived at their figure
phrases: “Could I think it over until tomorrow?”
“If we land there — could we review the salary again in six months?”

closing.title: Closing
closing.description: Make sure what you agreed is written down.
tips: Summarise out loud what you have agreed
Ask for it in writing: salary, hours, start date, any follow-up
Say thank you whatever the outcome — you will be working together
Write down your own impressions afterwards, while they are fresh
phrases: “So we say … kronor from …, is that right?”
“Could you send that in writing so I have it?”

do.title: Do this
items: Have a range in mind, not a single figure
Talk about the work and what you contribute
Ask questions and listen to the end
Take time to think if you get unsure
Decide your lowest level in advance
Ask for the agreement in writing

dont.title: Avoid
items: Saying yes straight away to the first offer
Justifying the salary with your private finances
Comparing yourself with named colleagues
Giving ultimatums you will not stand behind
Apologising for raising the subject of pay
Forgetting everything but the money — hours and training are worth something too

scenarios.title: Practise a situation
scenarios.intro: Four common situations. No figures here — they depend entirely on occupation, place and employer.

firstJob.title: First job after a long time out of work
firstJob.description: You have an offer and need to say what salary you want.
firstJob.advice: Having been away from work does not lower what the job is worth. Start from what the role normally pays and ask in line with that — not below it to be accommodating. Where there is a collective agreement, the minimum is a floor, not a target. If you are unsure: ask for time to think and call the union the same day.

offer.title: You have a job offer
offer.description: They have mentioned a salary and you can respond before signing.
offer.advice: Thank them and ask to come back tomorrow. Check the level against a real source. If you want more, name a figure and one sentence on why, and mention what you bring to the role. Also ask when pay is next reviewed.

annual.title: The annual salary review
annual.description: You have been there a while and want a raise.
annual.advice: Start from what has changed since last time: new duties, more responsibility, things you solved. Write three examples in advance. If the answer is no, ask what it would take for a yes, and agree when you will revisit it.

newDuties.title: Your duties have grown
newDuties.description: The job has expanded but the salary has not.
newDuties.advice: Describe what has been added and what it means in practice. Growing duties is in itself a sound reason to talk about pay — you do not have to wait for the annual review to raise it.

tips.title: One tip
items: Avoid naming the first figure if you can — ask what they had in mind instead.
If you are pushed for a figure: give a range and say what it depends on.
Find out whether the workplace has a collective agreement. It affects both pay and conditions.
Silence is not yours to fill. It is fine to think for a few seconds.
Ask when pay is next reviewed — a date is part of the negotiation too.
If you are in a union: call them before the meeting, not after.
